common-indian-toad.name: Common Indian toad
common-indian-toad.about: A toad of gardens, farmland and towns that breeds in the monsoon, when its black tadpoles fill pools. Young toads appear in large numbers as the rains end.

green-frog.name: Green frog
green-frog.about: A largely aquatic frog of ponds, tanks and paddy fields, rarely found far from water.

painted-frog.name: Painted frog
painted-frog.about: A plump, burrowing frog that hides by day in soil or leaf litter and feeds on ants and termites. Frogs like this breed at the start of the rains, when males call from pools.

bar-headed-goose.name: Bar-headed goose
bar-headed-goose.about: Breeds by mountain lakes in Central Asia and crosses the Himalaya to winter in India, often grazing on crop fields. Its blood carries oxygen unusually well, helping it fly at high altitude.
bar-headed-goose.range: Breeds in Central Asia; winters in South Asia, south to peninsular India

blue-bearded-bee-eater.name: Blue-bearded bee-eater
blue-bearded-bee-eater.about: A large bee-eater of forest clearings in the hills rather than open country. Its long blue throat feathers can be fluffed out into the beard that gives it its name.
blue-bearded-bee-eater.range: Indian subcontinent and parts of South-east Asia

blue-tailed-bee-eater.name: Blue-tailed bee-eater
blue-tailed-bee-eater.about: Usually seen near water, catching bees, wasps and dragonflies in flight and beating them on a perch before swallowing. It nests in colonies, digging tunnels into sandy riverbanks.

collared-dove.name: Eurasian collared dove
collared-dove.about: The same dove that spread across Europe in the 20th century, reaching Britain in 1952. Its Latin name decaocto, Greek for 'eighteen', imitates its three-note coo.
collared-dove.range: Europe, North Africa and Asia; introduced in North America

dusky-eagle-owl.name: Dusky eagle-owl
dusky-eagle-owl.about: A large grey-brown owl with ear tufts, often found in old trees near water, villages and roadside avenues. It nests in the old stick nests of other large birds.
dusky-eagle-owl.range: Pakistan and India east to South-east Asia

himalayan-whistling-thrush.name: Blue whistling thrush
himalayan-whistling-thrush.about: A dark violet-blue thrush spangled with paler blue, found along mountain streams, where it feeds on snails, crabs and insects. Its loud, human-like whistling song is heard at dawn and dusk.
himalayan-whistling-thrush.range: Mountains of Central and South Asia, including the Himalaya, to China and South-east Asia

hoopoe.name: Eurasian hoopoe
hoopoe.about: Strides over open ground, pausing to probe the soil with the full length of its long curved bill. Its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call is the likely source of its name.

indian-roller.name: Indian roller
indian-roller.about: Often perches on roadside wires and trees in open country; the blue in its wings looks dull at rest but vivid in flight. It is the state bird of three Indian states.
indian-roller.range: West Asia to the Indian subcontinent

white-throated-kingfisher.name: White-throated kingfisher
white-throated-kingfisher.about: Often hunts far from water, taking crabs, lizards, frogs, rodents and even small birds. In the breeding season males call loudly in the early morning from rooftops, wires and other high perches.
white-throated-kingfisher.range: From the Sinai east through the Indian subcontinent to China and Indonesia

legge-s-hawk-eagle.name: Legge's hawk-eagle
legge-s-hawk-eagle.about: A large crested forest eagle of south-west India and Sri Lanka, formerly treated as a race of the mountain hawk-eagle. It can take prey as heavy as an Indian peafowl.
legge-s-hawk-eagle.size: 67–86 cm long; females larger than males

lesser-yellownape-woodpecker.name: Lesser yellownape
lesser-yellownape-woodpecker.about: Named for the bright yellow tuft on its nape; males also show red above the eye and a red moustache. It can dart out its long tongue to catch insects.

montagu-s-harrier.name: Montagu's harrier
montagu-s-harrier.about: Named after the British naturalist George Montagu. Birds from the east of its breeding range winter in India, hunting low and buoyantly over grassland and crops along regular routes.
montagu-s-harrier.range: Breeds across Europe and Central Asia; winters in Africa and the Indian subcontinent

mottled-wood-owl.name: Mottled wood owl
mottled-wood-owl.about: A large owl without ear tufts, its face marked with fine concentric barring. Pairs are most vocal at dawn and dusk, when male and female call together in a duet.
mottled-wood-owl.range: Mainly India, in groves, gardens and open woodland

osprey.name: Osprey
osprey.about: A fish specialist that hovers, then plunges feet first, gripping prey with a reversible outer toe. It winters across South Asia; one bird tagged in Norway was tracked to western India.
osprey.range: Almost worldwide; a winter visitor across South Asia

indian-paradise-flycatcher.name: Indian paradise flycatcher
indian-paradise-flycatcher.about: Adult males grow tail streamers up to 30 cm long and come in rufous and white forms; females and young males are rufous and short-tailed.
indian-paradise-flycatcher.size: 19–22 cm long; adult males add tail streamers up to 30 cm
indian-paradise-flycatcher.range: Indian subcontinent, with breeding populations north into Central Asia

indian-peafowl.name: Indian peafowl
indian-peafowl.about: India's national bird. The male's train is not its tail but elongated upper tail coverts, moulted each year after the monsoon and regrown by about February.
indian-peafowl.size: Males about 1.0–1.2 m long, or 2.0–2.3 m including the train; females about 95 cm
indian-peafowl.range: Native to the Indian subcontinent; introduced elsewhere

pied-cuckoo.name: Pied cuckoo
pied-cuckoo.about: In India its arrival has long been seen as a sign of the coming monsoon. It is a brood parasite, laying its eggs mainly in the nests of babblers, which raise the chick.

plain-prinia.name: Plain prinia
plain-prinia.about: A small, long-tailed warbler that skulks in tall grass, reeds and scrub, usually given away by its repetitive 'tlee-tlee-tlee' song. Its tail is longer in winter than in the breeding season.
plain-prinia.range: Pakistan and India to southern China and South-east Asia

purple-heron.name: Purple heron
purple-heron.about: More secretive than the grey heron, it skulks in reedbeds and waits motionless for fish and frogs. Its long toes let it walk across floating vegetation.

red-whiskered-bulbul.name: Red-whiskered bulbul
red-whiskered-bulbul.about: A crested bulbul with a red patch behind the eye and a red vent, common in hill forests and gardens. Introduced populations live as far afield as Australia, Mauritius and Florida.
red-whiskered-bulbul.range: Tropical Asia; introduced in several other countries

indian-rock-eagle-owl.name: Indian eagle-owl
indian-rock-eagle-owl.about: A large horned owl of rocky hills, ravines and scrub, usually seen in pairs. Its deep, resonant two-note call carries at dusk in the breeding season.
indian-rock-eagle-owl.range: Indian subcontinent, south of the Himalaya

sri-lanka-bay-owl.name: Sri Lanka bay owl
sri-lanka-bay-owl.about: A small, strictly nocturnal owl of humid evergreen forest with a heart-shaped facial disc. It is so secretive in the Western Ghats that its presence is often detected only when an injured bird is found.
sri-lanka-bay-owl.range: Western Ghats (mainly south of Goa) and Sri Lanka

woolly-necked-stork.name: Asian woolly-necked stork
woolly-necked-stork.about: Mostly feeds in farmland and unprotected wetlands rather than reserves. Surveys showing it was far commoner in South Asia than once thought led to its downlisting from Vulnerable to Near Threatened.

baronet.name: Baronet
baronet.about: Its caterpillars feed on sal and on tendu (Diospyros melanoxylon), the tree whose leaves are used to roll beedis. The green caterpillar carries long, feathery spines along each side.
baronet.range: Lower Himalaya to southern India; Sri Lanka

common-map.name: Common map
common-map.about: Named for the fine black lines on its pale wings, which look like a map. It drinks at damp ground and has been recorded migrating in southern India.
common-map.range: Hill forests from the Himalaya to the far south of India, east to China and Japan; avoids the dry plains

crimson-tip.name: Crimson tip
crimson-tip.about: A small white butterfly with a red patch on each forewing tip, very variable in colour, especially in females. Its caterpillars feed on caper-family shrubs such as Capparis, Cadaba and Maerua.
crimson-tip.range: Africa, Arabia and Iran to western and southern India and Sri Lanka

large-salmon-arab.name: Large salmon Arab
large-salmon-arab.about: Males are paler in desert areas and darker where rain is regular. In India its caterpillars have been recorded on caper-family shrubs such as Cadaba fruticosa; elsewhere on Capparis.
large-salmon-arab.range: Eastern Mediterranean and Arabia east to India and Sri Lanka

common-leopard-butterfly.name: Common leopard
common-leopard-butterfly.about: A sun-loving butterfly that basks with its wings spread wide and often drinks in groups at damp ground. It is absent from the wettest parts of India during the monsoon.
common-leopard-butterfly.range: Sub-Saharan Africa and South and Southeast Asia, up to 3,000 m in the Himalaya

southern-birdwing.name: Southern birdwing
southern-birdwing.about: Its caterpillars feed on Aristolochia vines and store their toxins, so the adults are distasteful to predators. Adults glide high over clearings and come down to flowers such as Ixora and Lantana.
southern-birdwing.range: Western Ghats and other parts of southern India

tawny-coster.name: Tawny coster
tawny-coster.about: A slow, low flier that predators avoid: it is distasteful and, when attacked, plays dead and oozes a foul yellow fluid. Its caterpillars feed on passion flowers and other toxic plants.
tawny-coster.range: South and Southeast Asia; recently reached Australia

yellow-pansy.name: Yellow pansy
yellow-pansy.about: Males carry a brilliant blue spot on each hindwing, set in black. It is usually seen in open scrub and grassland.
yellow-pansy.range: Africa and tropical Asia, including India

black-faced-langur.name: Grey langur
black-faced-langur.about: Grey langurs live in troops that feed mainly on leaves, on the ground as well as in trees. Chital often stay close to them, and the two species respond to each other's alarm calls.
black-faced-langur.size: Head-body 51–79 cm, with a tail longer than the body

blackbuck.name: Blackbuck
blackbuck.about: An antelope of open grassy plains, usually seen in herds. Mature males turn dark brown to black and carry long corkscrew horns; females are fawn and usually hornless.

chital-herd.name: Chital
chital-herd.about: Chital herds are loose and change membership often, and only stags carry antlers. Females and young bark persistently when they spot a predator, which often tells guides where to look.
chital-herd.size: Shoulder height: stags 90–100 cm, hinds 65–75 cm
chital-herd.range: India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka

asian-elephant.name: Asian elephant
asian-elephant.about: Asia's largest land animal. Females and calves move in small groups of related cows linked by loose social networks, while adult bulls live alone or in temporary bachelor groups.
asian-elephant.size: Shoulder height: bulls about 2.75 m, cows about 2.4 m

asian-elephant-tusker.name: Asian elephant
asian-elephant-tusker.about: Only Asian bull elephants grow large tusks. Cows have none, or small 'tushes' seen only when the mouth is open, and some bulls, called makhnas, are tuskless too.
asian-elephant-tusker.size: Bulls weigh about 4 tonnes on average

nilgiri-tahr.name: Nilgiri tahr
nilgiri-tahr.about: A wild mountain goat of the grassy slopes and cliffs of the southern Western Ghats. Herds feed in the mornings and evenings and rest on ridges by day; Eravikulam holds the largest population. Adult males like this one are darker than females, with a pale saddle patch on the back, which is why they are called 'saddlebacks'.
nilgiri-tahr.size: Males about 100 cm at the shoulder
nilgiri-tahr.range: Nilgiri and Anamalai hills, southern Western Ghats

indian-gaur.name: Gaur
indian-gaur.about: The largest of the wild cattle, dark brown with white or tan lower legs and a high ridge behind the shoulders. Where undisturbed, herds feed by day and are led by an old female.
indian-gaur.size: Average shoulder height 1.68 m (cows) to 1.88 m (bulls)

indian-giant-squirrel.name: Indian giant squirrel
indian-giant-squirrel.about: A large, multicoloured squirrel of the upper canopy that rarely comes down to the ground. It leaps up to 6 m between trees and builds its nests high in tall trees.
indian-giant-squirrel.size: Head-body 25–50 cm, tail about as long or longer
indian-giant-squirrel.range: Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats and central India

indian-leopard.name: Indian leopard
indian-leopard.about: Where tigers are present, leopards take smaller prey and keep to the margins between prime tiger habitat and village land. They are agile climbers, and sightings are often brief.
indian-leopard.size: Males about 50–77 kg, females about 29–34 kg

lion-tailed-macaque.name: Lion-tailed macaque
lion-tailed-macaque.about: A black rainforest macaque with a grey or silver mane framing the face and a tufted, lion-like tail. Troops are usually seen high in the canopy of evergreen forest and are active only by day.

slender-loris.name: Slender loris
slender-loris.about: A small primate that is active only at night, moving slowly and deliberately along thin branches. In southern India it is often found in acacia and tamarind scrub near farmland.

sloth-bear.name: Sloth bear
sloth-bear.about: A shaggy black bear that feeds largely on termites and ants. It has no upper incisors and long, mobile lips for sucking up insects, and mothers carry young cubs on their backs.

smooth-coated-otter.name: Smooth-coated otter
smooth-coated-otter.about: Lives in groups of up to 11 along rivers, lakes and reservoirs, feeding mainly on fish. On the Moyar River below the Nilgiris it favours rocky, fast-flowing stretches with sandy banks.
smooth-coated-otter.range: South and Southeast Asia, with an isolated population in Iraq

stripe-necked-mongoose.name: Stripe-necked mongoose
stripe-necked-mongoose.about: A mongoose with a dark stripe down the side of the neck. It is active by day and feeds on frogs, crabs, rodents, reptiles and birds, and sometimes on larger prey such as mouse deer and hares.

bengal-tiger-on-the-move.name: Bengal tiger
bengal-tiger-on-the-move.about: Adult tigers are solitary and patrol home ranges that they scent-mark. On safari, the alarm barks of chital and the calls of langurs are often the first sign that one is moving nearby.

tiger-cub-resting.name: Bengal tiger
tiger-cub-resting.about: Young tigers stay with their mother for up to about two years, learning to hunt, before leaving to find territories of their own.

tiger-cub.name: Bengal tiger
tiger-cub.about: A cub can make its first kill at around 11 months, but it stays with its mother until 18–24 months old. Young males tend to become independent earlier than females.
tiger-cub.size: Adult males in central India average about 190 kg

tigress-with-cubs.name: Bengal tiger
tigress-with-cubs.about: A tigress raises her cubs alone, usually two or three to a litter. They stay with her for about two years, then leave her home range to set up their own.
tigress-with-cubs.size: Adult females in central India average about 132 kg

bengal-tiger.name: Bengal tiger
bengal-tiger.about: The 2022 estimate put India's wild tigers at 3,167–3,682, with smaller populations in Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Each adult holds a home range that it scent-marks.
bengal-tiger.size: Total length with tail: males 2.8–3.1 m, females 2.6–2.9 m

atlas-moth.name: Atlas moth
atlas-moth.about: Adults have no working mouthparts and live only briefly on fat stored as caterpillars. The hooked forewing tips resemble snake heads, and wing movements make the likeness stronger.

indian-moon-moth.name: Indian moon moth
indian-moon-moth.about: Adults have no working mouthparts and live only about a week. Its caterpillars feed on many trees and shrubs, including rhododendron, cherry, walnut and sweetgum.
indian-moon-moth.range: India east to Japan, south to Sri Lanka and Borneo

bamboo-forest.name: Bamboo forest
bamboo-forest.about: Bamboos are giant grasses that grow in clumps within moist and dry deciduous forest. Many species flower only after decades, often all together, and then die back.
bamboo-forest.range: Moist and dry deciduous forests across India
bamboo-forest.feature: Male bamboo (Dendrocalamus strictus), common in dry forest, grows 6–18 m tall

dry-deciduous-forest.name: Dry deciduous forest
dry-deciduous-forest.about: Trees such as teak, axlewood (Anogeissus latifolia) and Indian frankincense (Boswellia serrata) drop their leaves through the dry winter and spring. Most rain falls in the June to September monsoon.
dry-deciduous-forest.range: Deccan Plateau and central India, in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats
dry-deciduous-forest.feature: Home to tiger, dhole, sloth bear and gaur in central India

indian-coral-tree.name: Indian coral tree
indian-coral-tree.about: A thorny, deciduous tree that flowers in late winter or early spring, before its new leaves appear, with dense clusters of crimson flowers.
indian-coral-tree.range: East Africa and the Indian subcontinent to northern Australia and Fiji

evergreen-forest.name: Evergreen forest
evergreen-forest.about: Tall, many-layered forest that keeps its canopy all year. In the Western Ghats it grows on the rain-soaked western slopes, which take the full force of the south-west monsoon.
evergreen-forest.range: Western Ghats, north-east India and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
evergreen-forest.feature: Closed canopy with no leafless season; Western Ghats rainfall ranges from about 1 to 9 m a year

flame-of-the-forest.name: Flame of the forest
flame-of-the-forest.about: Flowers in late winter and spring, after most of its leaves have fallen, though not every year. The orange-red flowers were once used to make colour for Holi.

glory-lily.name: Glory lily
glory-lily.about: A climber that grips with tendrils at its leaf tips and flowers in the rainy season. It is the state flower of Tamil Nadu, and most parts of the plant are highly poisonous.
glory-lily.size: Climbing stems up to 3–4 m long
glory-lily.range: Africa and tropical South and Southeast Asia

grassland-shola-mosaic.name: Grassland and shola mosaic
grassland-shola-mosaic.about: Shola forest fills the sheltered valleys and grassland covers the slopes. The mosaic is home to the Nilgiri tahr, and is threatened by wattle and eucalyptus spreading from plantations.
grassland-shola-mosaic.range: High ranges of the southern Western Ghats, such as the Nilgiris, Anamalai and Palani Hills
grassland-shola-mosaic.feature: Pollen from Nilgiri bogs suggests the mosaic existed 35,000 years ago

montane-shola-forest.name: Montane shola forest
montane-shola-forest.about: Patches of stunted evergreen forest in sheltered high valleys. Sholas hold water well and are the source of many Western Ghats streams and rivers.
montane-shola-forest.range: Southern and central Western Ghats, from the Nilgiris, Anamalai and Palani Hills to Kudremukh
montane-shola-forest.feature: Stunted montane forest, mostly above 2,000 m, locally down to about 1,600 m

nilgiri-rhododendron.name: Nilgiri rhododendron
nilgiri-rhododendron.about: Grows scattered in open high grassland, where it withstands strong winds and grass fires. It is thought to have reached these hills from the Himalaya during Ice Age cold periods.

bronze-backed-tree-snake.name: Bronze-backed tree snake
bronze-backed-tree-snake.about: A slender tree snake that is active by day and hunts geckos, lizards, frogs and small birds in the branches. It is not venomous and is harmless to people.
bronze-backed-tree-snake.range: India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Pakistan

indian-chameleon.name: Indian chameleon
indian-chameleon.about: A slow, swaying climber of shrubs and trees that catches insects with a long, sticky tongue. Like other chameleons it grips with tong-like feet and a prehensile tail, and moves each eye independently.
indian-chameleon.size: Body up to about 18 cm, plus a tail up to about 20 cm

common-skink.name: Common skink
common-skink.about: A sun-loving skink, active by day and often seen basking or foraging on rocks and open ground before slipping into cover. Several similar Eutropis species occur in India.

monitor-lizard.name: Monitor lizard
monitor-lizard.about: A large lizard that is active by day and often basks on a tree trunk or rock in the morning sun. Monitors have keen eyesight and usually move off well before people get close.

indian-star-tortoise.name: Indian star tortoise
indian-star-tortoise.about: A tortoise of dry country and scrub forest with a high, star-patterned shell that helps it roll back upright if turned over. Poaching for the pet trade led to full CITES Appendix I protection in 2019.

giant-wood-spider.name: Giant wood spider
giant-wood-spider.about: Females spin large vertical webs of golden-yellow silk, typically 0.5–1 m across. Males are tiny by comparison and easily overlooked.
giant-wood-spider.size: Female body up to 50 mm; males 4–10 times smaller
giant-wood-spider.range: South, East and Southeast Asia to Australia

indian-red-scorpion.name: Indian red scorpion
indian-red-scorpion.about: Nocturnal and often found in and around villages. Its sting is a medical emergency, especially for children, but hospital treatment with the drug prazosin has cut deaths sharply.
indian-red-scorpion.range: Most of India, eastern Pakistan and lowland Nepal; recently recorded in Sri Lanka

man-faced-stink-bug.name: Man-faced stink bug
man-faced-stink-bug.about: Named for the face-like pattern on its back. It gathers in large groups on shrubs; in the northern Western Ghats such groups have been recorded on Ixora and other forest plants.

bronze-frog.name: Bronze frog
bronze-frog.about: Frogs like this were once all called the bronzed frog. A 2014 study split them into several species: the true bronzed frog lives only in Sri Lanka, and Indian ones belong to related Indosylvirana species.

golden-backed-frog.name: Golden-backed frog
golden-backed-frog.about: One of several closely similar golden-backed frogs of southern India and Sri Lanka, usually found near water. Several were only described in 2014, and many are hard to name in the field.

broad-tailed-grassbird.name: Broad-tailed grassbird
broad-tailed-grassbird.about: A skulking warbler of tall grass on the higher hills. In the breeding season males rise into the air to sing a lark-like trill with a fluttering flight and fanned tail.
broad-tailed-grassbird.range: Montane grassland of the Western Ghats

flame-throated-bulbul.name: Flame-throated bulbul
flame-throated-bulbul.about: Goa's state bird, with a black head, white eye and orange-red throat. Small groups feed on berries and insects in evergreen forest, sometimes in mixed-species flocks.
flame-throated-bulbul.range: Western Ghats, from southern Maharashtra and Goa southwards

great-cormorant.name: Great cormorant
great-cormorant.about: Often seen perched with its wings spread after diving for fish. In the breeding season adults show white thigh patches and white plumes on the head and neck.
great-cormorant.range: Much of Europe, Asia and Africa, Australasia and the Atlantic coast of North America

great-indian-hornbill.name: Great hornbill
great-indian-hornbill.about: The female seals herself into a tree hollow to nest and is fed by the male through a narrow slit. Its heavy wingbeats can be heard from far off, a sound likened to a steam train.
great-indian-hornbill.range: Western Ghats and Himalayan foothills east through South-east Asia to Sumatra

malabar-grey-hornbill.name: Malabar grey hornbill
malabar-grey-hornbill.about: A small hornbill without a casque, usually in pairs or small groups feeding on figs. Its loud cackling and laughing calls are often the first sign of it in the forest.
malabar-grey-hornbill.range: Western Ghats, from about Nashik southwards

malabar-parakeet.name: Malabar parakeet
malabar-parakeet.about: Small flocks fly fast through forest clearings, giving screeching calls unlike those of other parakeets. Its bluish-grey plumage and long, yellow-tipped blue tail set it apart.
malabar-parakeet.range: Western Ghats and adjoining hills of south-west India

malabar-trogon.name: Malabar trogon
malabar-trogon.about: Perches still under the canopy, often with its back turned, so it is easily missed despite the male's crimson underparts. It feeds entirely on insects.
malabar-trogon.range: Western Ghats, hills of central India, parts of the Eastern Ghats, and Sri Lanka

malabar-whistling-thrush.name: Malabar whistling thrush
malabar-whistling-thrush.about: Known as the 'whistling schoolboy' for its very human-sounding whistled song at dawn. It feeds along rocky forest streams and usually nests in hollows on the stream bank.
malabar-whistling-thrush.range: Western Ghats and hills of peninsular India

nilgiri-flycatcher.name: Nilgiri flycatcher
nilgiri-flycatcher.about: A dark indigo-blue flycatcher of high shola forest that perches upright and flicks its tail while calling. It sallies out for insects, mostly from low perches; the female is duller.
nilgiri-flycatcher.range: Higher hills of the Western Ghats, mostly above 1,200 m

nilgiri-pipit.name: Nilgiri pipit
nilgiri-pipit.about: Restricted to short montane grassland with marshy patches, mostly above 1,000 to 1,500 m in the southern Western Ghats. It is richly coloured and heavily streaked for a pipit.
nilgiri-pipit.range: Montane grassland of the southern Western Ghats

nilgiri-wood-pigeon.name: Nilgiri wood pigeon
nilgiri-wood-pigeon.about: A large, dark pigeon of shola and evergreen forest, best identified by the black-and-white chequered patch on its nape. It feeds mainly on fruit in the forest canopy.
nilgiri-wood-pigeon.range: Hill ranges of the Western Ghats

white-bellied-treepie.name: White-bellied treepie
white-bellied-treepie.about: A long-tailed member of the crow family found in dense evergreen forest, often travelling with mixed flocks and greater racket-tailed drongos. When calling it bows and droops its wings.
white-bellied-treepie.range: Western Ghats, mainly south of Goa

white-bellied-woodpecker.name: White-bellied woodpecker
white-bellied-woodpecker.about: One of Asia's largest woodpeckers, also called the great black woodpecker. Its drumming and calls are louder than those of smaller woodpeckers, and it nests in large dead trees.

white-cheeked-barbet.name: White-cheeked barbet
white-cheeked-barbet.about: Its monotonous 'kot-roo, kot-roo' call becomes loud and constant in the breeding season. It feeds mainly on figs and chisels its nest hole in dead branches.
white-cheeked-barbet.range: Western Ghats and parts of the Eastern Ghats

yellow-throated-bulbul.name: Yellow-throated bulbul
yellow-throated-bulbul.about: A shy bulbul of steep, rocky, scrub-covered hills, mostly east of the Western Ghats, often detected by sudden cackling bursts of calls. Granite quarrying threatens parts of its habitat.
yellow-throated-bulbul.range: Rocky hills of southern peninsular India

asian-elephant-herd.name: Asian elephant
asian-elephant-herd.about: A family group is typically about three related adult females and their young. Calves are born after an 18–22 month pregnancy and suckle for up to three years; young bulls leave in adolescence.

indian-wild-dog.name: Dhole
indian-wild-dog.about: Dholes live in clans and hunt together, mostly in the early morning, and chital are a frequent prey. Several females may raise their pups in the same den.
indian-wild-dog.range: Much of India south of the Ganges; also East and Southeast Asia

jungle-cat.name: Jungle cat
jungle-cat.about: An unspotted, sandy to grey cat with short black tufts on its ears, found mainly in wetlands and dense waterside vegetation. Unlike most small cats it often hunts by day.
jungle-cat.size: About 36 cm at the shoulder; 2–16 kg
jungle-cat.range: Eastern Mediterranean to South and Southeast Asia

nilgiri-tahr-female.name: Nilgiri tahr
nilgiri-tahr-female.about: Females are smaller than males and stay paler. Both sexes have curved horns, up to about 30 cm long in females, and the young are usually born in January or February.
nilgiri-tahr-female.size: Horns up to about 30 cm in females
nilgiri-tahr-female.range: Nilgiri and Anamalai hills, southern Western Ghats

rhesus-macaque.name: Rhesus macaque
rhesus-macaque.about: A sociable macaque living in troops of 20 to 200, as much at home around temples and towns as in forest. Troops are built around families of related females.

ruddy-mongoose.name: Ruddy mongoose
ruddy-mongoose.about: A forest mongoose whose long tail has a dark tip, usually curved upwards and visible from a distance. It keeps to thick forest and edges but sometimes ventures into paddy fields and tea estates.

anaimalai-spiny-lizard.name: Anaimalai spiny lizard
anaimalai-spiny-lizard.about: A spiny-crested lizard of the high hills around Munnar, living at about 1,700–2,300 m in montane forest and in bushes, hedges and gardens.

forest-calotes.name: Forest calotes
forest-calotes.about: A tree-dwelling lizard of hill forests in peninsular India, active by day. In the breeding season, males turn brick-red on the head, nape and throat pouch.
forest-calotes.size: Up to 30 cm including the tail, usually about 25 cm
forest-calotes.range: Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats and Deccan hills

green-calotes.name: Green calotes
green-calotes.about: A large, bright green tree lizard, usually with white, cream or dark green crossbands on the body. Males develop a red head and throat in the breeding season.
green-calotes.range: Western Ghats, Shevaroy Hills and Sri Lanka

hump-nosed-pit-viper.name: Hump-nosed pit viper
hump-nosed-pit-viper.about: A small pit viper with an upturned snout that lies hidden in leaf litter by day and is active mainly at night. Its bite is medically important, so it is only watched with a guide, from a distance.

large-scaled-green-lizard.name: Large-scaled forest lizard
large-scaled-green-lizard.about: A large tree lizard of evergreen rainforest, found from Agumbe south to the Agasthyamalai hills. It is active by day and feeds on insects.
large-scaled-green-lizard.size: Snout to vent up to about 13.6 cm, plus a long tail

large-scaled-pit-viper.name: Large-scaled pit viper
large-scaled-pit-viper.about: A slow-moving, tree-climbing pit viper of the high hills, rarely found below 1,200 m, in rainforest and tea, coffee and cardamom estates. Venomous, so it is only watched with a guide, from a distance.
large-scaled-pit-viper.range: Southern Western Ghats, south of the Palghat Gap

malabar-pit-viper.name: Malabar pit viper
malabar-pit-viper.about: A pit viper of Western Ghats forest, active mainly at night but sometimes seen by day basking on rocks or branches near streams. Venomous, so it is only watched with a guide, from a distance.

saw-scaled-viper.name: Saw-scaled viper
saw-scaled-viper.about: A small viper of scrub, rock and sandy ground, active mostly at dusk and at night. One of India's 'big four' medically important snakes, so it is only ever watched with a guide, from a distance.
saw-scaled-viper.size: Usually under 60 cm, up to 80 cm
saw-scaled-viper.range: Indian subcontinent, Middle East and Central Asia
